inline.s: Each day Master Jiechen walked several circles around the old Master, and only after much difficulty did the seventh day arrive, when the old Master finally emerged from samadhi. He asked the old Master:

“While you were in samadhi, did you have awareness, or did you not? If you had awareness, then it could not be called entering samadhi; and if you had no awareness, would that not be a withered stillness—what is called ‘a dead water that cannot harbor a dragon?’”

You must know that this Dharma of the Chan school does not rest in samadhi as its ultimate; it seeks only to illumine the mind and see the nature. When true doubt is present before you, the mind is naturally pure. Because the gate of doubt is unbroken, it is not without knowing; and because there is no deluded thinking, it is not with knowing. Although there is no knowledge born of delusion, even a needle dropped upon the ground is heard with perfect clarity; each day you walked your circles around me and I knew it, only because of the power of the doubt, without giving rise to discrimination. Because no discrimination arises yet the doubt remains, the functioning continues unbroken, and so it is not withered stillness. Though it is not withered stillness, this is still but a matter along the course of practice, not yet the ultimate. That is why, over these seven days, I felt as if a finger-snap had passed away; had I entertained a single mind of discrimination, I would have come out of samadhi. Those who practice Chan must press this doubt to its utmost point; and when time and conditions arrive, and the mass of doubt is broken through, and one touches one’s own nostrils—that is truly the authentic accord with the birthless.
From then on, Master Jiechen followed the old Master wherever he went, holding him in deep faith and reverence.

Later, on one occasion, the old Master entered samadhi for eighteen days. When the others on the mountain learned of it, they all came to pay their respects to him. Finding this bothersome, the two of them shouldered their packs and set off for Mount Emei. One night they stayed in a small, abandoned, dilapidated temple. The old Master said that at midnight a flea bit Master Jiechen, who placed the flea upon the ground; when the flea toppled over it broke its leg, and the old Master, in samadhi, heard the flea crying out piteously. The next day the old Master questioned Master Jiechen about the matter, and when he heard it he was greatly astonished, thinking:
“That he should even know I set a flea upon the ground, and even hear its cries—such skill in samadhi is truly remarkable!”
From this one can see how inconceivable is the state in which body and mind have become pure.

Later the two of them went together to Yunnan to establish a practice center. At that time, in 1957, some of the senior masters of Yunju Mountain, aged over eighty, knew of these matters. They said that the old Master Jiechen was also quite extraordinary, for he later knew in advance the time of his passing, took leave of the community, and passed away seated in meditation.
